Q: Should I use std::rethrow_exception in my catch block, rather than directly rethrowing it? A:

std::rethrow_exception(std::current_exception()) will work in a function you call from a catch block, while throw; will only work within the catch block. (Of course, throw(e) will work anywhere).

If you have some common/shared "do I rethrow or handle this exception" logic, it might be useful.

If you have simple logic in a catch block and want to rethrow the current exception, the throw; (zero argument throw) idiom is probably what you want.

Q: Why does `Object.groupBy()` return an object where `hasOwnProperty` is not a function? A:

The groupBy method returns a so called null prototype object1. hasOwnProperty is a method of Object.prototype. A null prototype object has neither a prototype nor a constructor. So hasOwnproperty is not applicable to the return value.

1 The object you'd get using Object.create(null, [someObject])

You can however use the static method Object.hasOwn instead.

const people = [
    { name: "Ana", role: "dev" },
    { name: "Ben", role: "dev" },
    { name: "Cara", role: "pm" },
];

const grouped = Object.groupBy(people, (person) => person.role);
console.log(Object.hasOwn(grouped, "dev"));

Concerning the question why this choice is made: for groupBy one wants to avoid prototype pollution and return a clean key-value store without any inherited values. This also prevents malicious code trying to overwrite Object.prototype.

So in case of

const items = [
  { cat: 'toString', value: 1 },
  { cat: 'hasOwnProperty', value: 2 }
];
const grouped = Object.groupBy(items, item => item.cat);

grouped.hasOwnProperty refers to the grouped items, not Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty

Q: PHP 2d Array Declaration A:

All the answer so far use array() and/or aren't in one statement. You can use just square brackets to declare this if you wish:

protected array $requiredFieldsByReferenceType = [
    'Book' => ['volume' => true, 'source' => true],
    'Book Section' => ['volume' => true, 'source' => true],
    'Chart or Table' => ['volume' => true, 'source' => true],
];

Q: A method of iterating over the values of a list or a dictionary without a type conditional A:

Note: I don't think you should do this, I don't think there's anything wrong with being explicit about the fact that mappings are treated differently (and sets, arrays, tuples can't be represented in JSON anyway), but for the purposes of illustrating what the standard library supports:

One way you could do this is to create a Mapping implementation that's an iterable of its values, and use it when parsing the JSON into Python objects, as follows:

from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator, Mapping
from typing import Any, TypeVar

K = TypeVar("K")
V = TypeVar("V")


class ValuesIterable(Mapping[K, V]):

    _data: dict[K, V]

    def __init__(self, pairs: Iterable[tuple[K, V]]):
        self._data = dict(pairs)

    def __getitem__(self, key: K) -> V:
        return self._data[key]

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[Any]:  # note
        yield from self._data.values()

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._data)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import json

    data = '{"foo": 123, "bar": 456}'
    document: ValuesIterable[str, int] = json.loads(data, object_pairs_hook=ValuesIterable)
    print(list(document))  # -> [123, 456]

Per the docs:

object_pairs_hook is an optional function that will be called with the result of every JSON object decoded with an ordered list of pairs. The return value of object_pairs_hook will be used instead of the dict. This feature can be used to implement custom decoders.

However, note that a Mapping[K, V] is usually an Iterable[K], not an Iterable[V] (list(document) would be inferred as list[str], although it's actually list[int]). This implementation has some counter-intuitive semantics, like key in document potentially giving a different result to key in list(document), violating the Liskov substitution principle.
